Hierarchy 1 description en: rock type that has been formed from solidified magma through either extrusive or intrusive processes. The character of igneous rock is affected by the chemical constitution of the magma and the rate at which the magma cools. The magma will have a molten temperature between 800°C and 1200°C. When solidified, it crystallizes into a mass of mineral crystals. The main minerals of igneous rocks are quartz, feldspar, muscovite, biotite, and mafics. Extrusive igneous rocks are formed when the magma flows out onto the surface of the land or into the sea, and cools very rapidly. The resulting rock (e.g. obsidian) will be glassy or have very fine crystal grains where minerals have crystallized. Intrusive igneous rocks are formed when the magma is injected into other rocks to form dykes, sills, batholiths, plutons, and stocks. The resulting rock (e.g. granite) is often very coarse-grained as cooling is slower, giving larger mineral crystals time to form.

A type of rock that is formed by the deposition and compression of particles of rocks that have been eroded from the land (clastic sedimentary rocks), organic materials (organic sedimentary rocks), or chemicals that are deposited from water (chemical precipitates).

Any rock that has been altered by metamorphism, involving heating and pressure. Also known as tertiary rock because metamorphic rock is derived from primary igneous rocks and secondary sedimentary rocks.
 denoting or relating to rock that has undergone transformation by heat, pressure, or other natural agencies, e.g. in the folding of strata or the nearby  intrusion of igneous rocks.
